samples.summary: Session/refresh cookie `Secure` flag is now derived from `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL`'s scheme, so a misconfigured `http://` callback on a TLS-fronted deployment silently drops `Secure` from the session token
samples.evidence: `baseCookieOptions()` changed from `secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production'` to `secure: secureCookies(this.configService)` (auth.controller.ts:528). `secureCookies` (github-auth.guard.ts:91-98) returns `false` for *any* `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL` starting with `http://`, and that branch is checked before the `NODE_ENV==='production'` fallback. Previously a production deployment always got `Secure` session/refresh cookies regardless of that variable. Now a deployment that terminates TLS at a proxy and leaves `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL=http://...` (the exact spelling the self-hosting guide prints, packages/documentation/developers/self-hosting.md:121) serves `wafflebase_session` / `wafflebase_refresh` without `Secure` on an https site — the JWT then rides any plaintext request to the origin and is trivially stolen by a network attacker or a downgrade link. The reasoning in the comment (a Secure cookie on an http origin is dropped) is sound for a genuinely-http origin, but the predicate reads a config string, not the actual serving scheme, so one wrong env value silently removes a transport control from the session cookie rather than only from the 5-minute login cookie. Consider keeping `secure: true` whenever `NODE_ENV==='production'` OR the callback is https, and only relaxing for loopback.

samples.summary: The browser login flow's new CSRF state cookie loses its only anti-planting control (`__Host-`) on plain-http non-loopback deployments, while the CLI flow refuses to run there — the forced-login CSRF this change exists to close stays open on exactly the deployment the self-hosting docs describe
samples.evidence: `cliLoginAvailable()` (github-auth.guard.ts:142-144) refuses `?mode=cli` on a plain-http non-loopback origin precisely because its gate is a plantable cookie. No equivalent guard exists for the browser flow: `canActivate` falls through to `issueLoginCookie(context, OAUTH_STATE_COOKIE)` at github-auth.guard.ts:510-516 unconditionally. On such a deployment `loginCookieName` returns the bare `wafflebase_oauth_state` (github-auth.guard.ts:165), and `stateSignature`'s own doc-comment states the signature is *not* a defence against cookie planting because one unauthenticated `GET /auth/github` publishes a matching (cookie, state) pair. So a sibling subdomain — or anyone on the cleartext path — plants the cookie half, replays the harvested `state`, and completes `GET /auth/github/callback` with their own GitHub code: the victim's browser is issued session cookies for the attacker's account (forced-login CSRF), which `verifyCallbackState` (auth.controller.ts:297-312) then accepts. packages/documentation/developers/self-hosting.md:121 still documents `http://your-domain:3000/auth/github/callback` as a supported production setup. The degradation is documented in docs/design/backend.md but nothing in the code warns, logs, or refuses.

samples.summary: `nonce` is length-bounded only, with no charset restriction, unlike `code_challenge` — arbitrary 128-byte attacker-chosen bytes are stored and echoed into a `Location` header and an HTML page
samples.evidence: `boundedToken(req.query?.nonce, 1, MAX_NONCE_LENGTH)` (github-auth.guard.ts:463) passes no `pattern`, while `code_challenge` two lines down is pinned to `/^[A-Za-z0-9\-._~]+$/` (line 472). The stored nonce reaches two sinks: `&state=${encodeURIComponent(cliState.nonce)}` in the loopback `Location` (auth.controller.ts:262) and the consent page's Continue href via `URLSearchParams` + `escapeHtml` (auth.controller.ts:169-176). Both encode today, so I could not build a working header-injection or XSS chain — but the file's own comment claims CLI-supplied values are 'restricted to the base64url alphabet so nothing that lands in a redirect URL or a log line can carry structure', and for the nonce that is not true. Any future sink that interpolates the nonce without encoding (a log line, an error message, a template) becomes injectable. Apply the same base64url pattern.

samples.summary: `ERROR_MESSAGES[error]` indexes a plain object with an attacker-controlled query value, so inherited `Object.prototype` members (`toString`, `constructor`, `valueOf`) are returned instead of falling through to the fallback
samples.evidence: `const error = searchParams.get("error")` then `{ERROR_MESSAGES[error] ?? FALLBACK_ERROR}`. `ERROR_MESSAGES` is an object literal, so `?error=toString` yields `Object.prototype.toString` (a function, not `undefined`), the `??` fallback never fires, and a function is passed as a React child. That is at best a rendered-nothing + console error and at worst a render throw on a page an attacker can link a victim to. Use `Object.hasOwn(ERROR_MESSAGES, error)` or a `Map`. Note packages/frontend has no `tsc` lane, so nothing else catches this.

samples.summary: OAuth `state` is validated only after passport has already exchanged GitHub's authorization code for a token, so an unauthenticated caller can drive the server's outbound token exchange with no CSRF binding checked
samples.evidence: `@UseGuards(AuthGuard('github'))` on `githubAuthCallback` (auth.controller.ts:216) runs the strategy — and therefore the server-to-server code→token POST to GitHub with the app's `client_secret` — before `verifyCallbackState` at line 226. Because `GitHubStrategy.authenticate` only sets the `state` option on the *outbound* request, passport-oauth2 keeps a `NullStore` whose `verify` always succeeds (documented at github.strategy.ts:56-59), so nothing at the guard layer checks state either. The impact is bounded (10 req/60s throttle, fixed `tokenURL`, and no user record is touched before validation), but the CSRF check should precede the credential-consuming exchange rather than follow it.

samples.summary: `logSafeUrl`'s path-secret redaction matches only exact three-segment shapes, so any global route prefix or route relocation silently un-redacts share-link and invite tokens in the access log
samples.evidence: `redactPathSecrets` bails with `if (rule.shape.length !== normalized.length) continue;` (log-safe-url.ts:110). I confirmed there is no `setGlobalPrefix` in packages/backend/src/main.ts today, so the two rules currently fire. But the moment a prefix is added (or `/api/v1` grows a share-resolve variant) the segment count changes and `GET /share-links/<token>/resolve` / `POST /invites/<token>/accept` log their credential verbatim — the invite one at `info` on success, per `customLogLevel` in app.module.ts:49-61. A suffix/`indexOf`-anchored match, or a lint against the route decorators, would fail closed instead.

samples.summary: `login-url.txt` (which holds this login's nonce, port and PKCE challenge) is created with `mode: 0o600` but never `chmod`'d afterwards, unlike `session.json`, and its parent directory is created with the default umask
samples.evidence: `rmSync(file, {force:true}); writeFileSync(file, url, {mode: 0o600})` (login.ts:227-228). `mode` only applies at creation, so the preceding `rmSync` is the whole of the guarantee — and `rmSync` can fail on a directory the user cannot unlink from, leaving an existing world-readable file to be overwritten with its old permissions. `packages/cli/src/config/session.ts:68-70` handles the same hazard with an explicit `chmodSync(path, 0o600)` after the write; this new file does not. `mkdirSync(dirname(file), {recursive:true})` (login.ts:224) also passes no `mode`, so `~/.wafflebase` is created 0755. Anyone who reads this file can start their own login against the same nonce/challenge and push an authorization code at the CLI's port (RFC 8252 §8.9), which is the attack the rest of the file is built to stop.

samples.summary: `bindingSecret` uses `??` rather than `||`, so an empty-string `JWT_SECRET` bypasses the ephemeral fallback and reaches `hkdfSync` with zero-length key material
samples.evidence: `const base = configService.get<string>('JWT_SECRET') ?? EPHEMERAL_BINDING_SECRET;` (github-auth.guard.ts:265-266). `''` is neither null nor undefined, so it is used as the HKDF ikm at line 271; Node's `crypto.hkdfSync` requires the key to be at least one byte, so every `GET /auth/github` would throw a 500 rather than fall back. Fail-closed, but it is an availability cliff on a plausible `.env` typo (`JWT_SECRET=`), and the sibling `OAUTH_STATE_SECRET` read one line above correctly uses truthiness.

verdict.reason: The code is exactly as described. auth.controller.ts:515-531 sets session/refresh cookie options with `secure: secureCookies(this.configService)` (line 528), replacing a NODE_ENV-based predicate per its own comment (518-525). github-auth.guard.ts:91-98 returns `false` for ANY `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL` beginning with `http://` (line 96), and that branch is evaluated before the `NODE_ENV === 'production'` fallback (line 97), so an http callback string overrides production. `secureCookies` deliberately ignores the live request scheme (comment 71-73), so a TLS-terminating proxy deployment (main.ts:35-41 supports BACKEND_TRUST_PROXY) that leaves an http callback serves `wafflebase_session`/`wafflebase_refresh` without `Secure` on an https origin. I found no guard anywhere that rejects or normalizes an http callback URL at startup — no config validation schema exists in packages/backend/src (searched for validationSchema/Joi; only app.module.ts:87 uses NODE_ENV, for logging). The misconfiguration is the exact spelling the self-hosting guide prints for a non-localhost domain (self-hosting.md:121, also README.md:126, packages/backend/README.md:41); the surrounding prose (self-hosting.md:124-131) warns about https but does not prevent it and only discusses login/CLI cookies, not the session JWT. This is a weakened transport control on a session credential — in-lane for the security rubric and blocking at major severity.

verdict.reason: The mechanics are as described — no browser-flow equivalent of cliLoginAvailable exists (github-auth.guard.ts:510-516), no config validation or startup warning exists (app.module.ts:27, main.ts), and __Host- is dropped on plain http (github-auth.guard.ts:161-166) — but it is not a blocking security defect. The attack presumes an adversary who can write cookies on the deployment origin; that adversary already achieves the identical forced-login outcome far more simply, because the session cookie itself is un-prefixed on every deployment: `wafflebase_session` (auth.controller.ts:59) is set via baseCookieOptions() with no __Host- prefix (auth.controller.ts:484-490, 515-531) and accepted verbatim by JwtStrategy (jwt.strategy.ts:11-16). The attacker plants their own session JWT directly; the OAuth-state path grants no incremental capability, so refusing the browser flow on plain http would close nothing. Against the adversary the state cookie actually exists to stop — the ordinary web attacker who can only cause navigations — the check at auth.controller.ts:297-311 still holds on plain http, so this is not a gate that "reads as covered" while being bypassable. The reviewer's documentation evidence is also inaccurate: self-hosting.md:124-131 explicitly directs operators to https, explains that only https yields Secure/__Host-, and states the plain-http degradation in plain language, as does packages/backend/README.md:100-105 — the posture is documented, not silent. Prefixing the session/state cookies or logging a startup warning is a reasonable hardening item at minor severity, not a major merge blocker.

finding.summary: New path-segment redaction misses the workspace invite token (`POST /invites/:token/accept`), which is logged verbatim
finding.evidence: `SECRET_PATH_SEGMENTS` (log-safe-url.ts:79) lists exactly one shape: `['share-links','*','resolve']`. But `packages/backend/src/workspace/workspace.controller.ts:117` exposes `POST invites/:token/accept`, where the path segment IS the credential — holding it lets any authenticated account join the workspace. `logSafeUrl` leaves that path untouched (it is not under `/auth`, and no rule matches), so the pino `req` serializer wired in at `app.module.ts:70` writes the live invite token into the access log. Worse than the share-link case the change fixed: `customLogLevel` (app.module.ts:49-60) logs non-GET mutations at `info` (so *successful* accepts too) and any 4xx at `warn` (an expired/revoked/already-a-member attempt), so both the working and the failing token land in the log. Attack: anyone with read access to the access log (operators, log shippers, an agent harness transcript) lifts a still-valid invite token and accepts it into a workspace they were never invited to. This is exactly the class of gap the change's own commentary claims to have closed ("grep for the credential's *other* carriers before calling it covered").

verdict.reason: The finding claims SECRET_PATH_SEGMENTS lists exactly one shape (share-links/*/resolve) and therefore leaves POST /invites/:token/accept unredacted. That is factually wrong in this tree: log-safe-url.ts:91-94 contains TWO entries, the second being { shape: ['invites', '*', 'accept'], index: 1 } at line 93 — exactly the rule said to be missing. The surrounding doc comment (log-safe-url.ts:72-76) explicitly justifies it with the same customLogLevel info-on-success reasoning the finding uses. redactPathSecrets (log-safe-url.ts:97-121) normalizes (decode, lowercase, drop empty segments) and blanks segment index 1, and logSafeUrl invokes it on every non-/auth path (log-safe-url.ts:175). Route shape matches: workspace.controller.ts:117 is @Post('invites/:token/accept') and there is no setGlobalPrefix anywhere in packages/backend, so the logged path is /invites/<token>/accept — 3 segments, satisfying rule.shape.length === normalized.length. Dedicated regression tests assert the redaction, including case-variant and double-slash spellings (log-safe-url.spec.ts:100-114), plus a negative test that /workspaces/:id/invites/:inviteId stays readable (log-safe-url.spec.ts:119-123). One counterexample suffices; this is a direct one.

finding.summary: `JWT_SECRET` is reused as the OAuth-state HMAC key, and one unauthenticated request hands an attacker a chosen-free (input, HMAC) pair for it
finding.evidence: `bindingSecret()` (line 176) returns `JWT_SECRET` — the same key `AuthModule`'s `JwtModule` signs and verifies session/refresh JWTs with (`auth.module.ts:19`) — and `stateSignature()` (line 195) publishes `HMAC-SHA256(JWT_SECRET, cookieValue)` as the `state` query parameter, while the *input* (`cookieValue`) is returned to the same caller in `Set-Cookie` by the same response (guard lines 359-365). So an unauthenticated `GET /auth/github` yields a verified plaintext/MAC pair under the JWT signing key. That is an offline brute-force oracle for `JWT_SECRET`: with a weak or guessable secret an attacker recovers it without ever creating an account or capturing a JWT, and then forges access tokens for any `sub` (full account takeover). Key separation is the fix (derive a distinct key, e.g. HKDF over `JWT_SECRET` with a `oauth-state` label, or a dedicated env var). The file's own comment argues at length about what the signature does and does not buy but never addresses the key reuse.

verdict.reason: The claimed code is not present. `bindingSecret()` (github-auth.guard.ts:261-276) does not return `JWT_SECRET`: it returns a dedicated `OAUTH_STATE_SECRET` when configured (262-263), otherwise an HKDF-SHA256-derived 32-byte subkey under the domain-separation label `wafflebase/oauth-login-binding/v1` (233, 271), falling back to an ephemeral random key when `JWT_SECRET` is unset (226, 266). The finding's cited line 176 is `secure: secureCookies(configService)` in `loginCookieOptions`, not a secret accessor. Every HMAC call site uses `bindingSecret` and none uses `JWT_SECRET` (512-515, 489-490, 543, auth.controller.ts:302); a repo-wide grep shows `JWT_SECRET` reaching only `auth.module.ts:19`, `auth.service.ts:51`, `jwt.strategy.ts:18` and tests. The claim that the comment "never addresses the key reuse" is also false — lines 238-259 and 294-295 discuss exactly this oracle and state key separation as the fix, and github-auth.guard.spec.ts:619-648 asserts `bindingSecret !== JWT_SECRET`, memoized determinism, and `OAUTH_STATE_SECRET` precedence. The exact remediation the finding requests (HKDF with an oauth-state label, or a dedicated env var) is already shipped in both forms. The only residual — that a guessable `JWT_SECRET` can still be tested through the derivation — is explicitly acknowledged (252-259) and is no worse than brute-forcing any HS256 JWT this server issues, so it is not the claimed key-reuse defect.

finding.summary: The CLI consent token authorizes *any* CLI parameters — it is not bound to the port/nonce/challenge the page displayed
finding.evidence: `issueLoginCookie(context, CLI_CONFIRM_COOKIE)` (line 342) mints a bare 32-byte random value with no association to the `port`, `nonce` or `code_challenge` of the consent request, and `hasConfirmation()` (lines 371-383) only compares the query half to the cookie half. So the gate proves "this browser was shown *some* CLI consent page in the last 5 minutes", not "this browser was shown the page naming port 9876". The whole documented defence is that the person read the port on the page they clicked; a confirm token obtained (or observed) for one set of parameters is spendable against a completely different `port=`, i.e. against an attacker-owned loopback listener, with no second consent page. Any leak of the token — it travels in a URL query string and therefore into browser history, and any future `Referrer-Policy` regression or non-`/auth` route prefix would put it in the access log — converts directly into the exact attack the interstitial exists to stop. I could not construct an end-to-end leak on the current code (the cookie is httpOnly, the page sets `<meta name="referrer" content="no-referrer">`, and `logSafeUrl` redacts `/auth` query strings), hence low confidence; the fix is cheap: HMAC the consent parameters into the token, or store `{token -> {port,nonce,codeChallenge}}` and require them to match on the confirmed request.

verdict.reason: The described code does not exist in this repository. The CLI consent token is NOT a bare copy of the random cookie value: at github-auth.guard.ts:487-494 the value from `issueLoginCookie(context, CLI_CONFIRM_COOKIE)` is fed as the keying input to `consentToken(bindingSecret(...), cookieValue, params)`, and `consentToken` (github-auth.guard.ts:332-346) HMAC-SHA256s the cookie value together with `port`, `nonce` and `codeChallenge`, each length-prefixed to prevent re-cutting. There is no `hasConfirmation()` function anywhere in the tree; the verifier is `matchedConfirmation` (github-auth.guard.ts:534-549), which recomputes the token from the *current request's* validated params (built at line 478) against each cookie binding using constant-time `secretEquals` (line 214-218). Therefore a confirmation minted for port 9876 does not verify against `port=4444`, which is the exact scenario the finding says is exploitable. Tests assert this directly: github-auth.guard.spec.ts:402 (token != cookie value), :403-409 (token == HMAC over displayed params), :471-485 ("refuses a confirmation minted for a different port"), :489 (different nonce or challenge). The finding's own suggested fix ("HMAC the consent parameters into the token") is already the implementation; its cited line numbers (342, 371-383) point at the parts array inside `consentToken` and at a doc comment, not at the code described.
